review: The refrain is Isa 49:15 (גַּם־אֵלֶּה תִשְׁכַּחְנָה וְאָנֹכִי לֹא אֶשְׁכָּחֵךְ) and is kept in the first person singular as His own promise, because the print puts it in quotation marks: the soul is quoting what the Lord said to her, not making a vow of her own.
1:1 doubles the refrain within one line, as the Arabic أَنَا لَا أَنْسَاكا أَنَا لَا أَنْسَاكا does; the doubling is the tune's opening and is not trimmed to a single occurrence.

2:2 רַגְלַי נוֹטְפוֹת דָּם — the Arabic تَنْزِفَ رِجْلَايَ دَما is 'my feet bleed blood'; נָטַף is the biblical verb for dripping (Judg 5:4, גַּם־שָׁמַיִם נָטָפוּ; Song 5:5, יָדַי נָטְפוּ מוֹר), kept because the stanza's image is blood dripping on the road and not a medical description.

3:3 וְהַהַבְטָחָה נִצֶּבֶת כַּצּוּר — the Arabic فَالْوَعْدُ رَاسٍ كَالْجَبَل is 'the promise stands firm as the mountain'; the Hebrew uses נִצֶּבֶת (Gen 28:12, נִצָּב) with צוּר rather than הַר, since צוּר is the psalm's word for the unmovable rock (Ps 18:3) and carries the theology the stanza needs.

4:1–2 וְיָבֹא אֵפוֹא כָּל־מָצָב / טוֹב יְהִי אוֹ רָע — the Arabic إِذًا لِيَأْتِ أَيُّ حَال / خَيْرًا يَكُونُ أَوْ وَبَال keeps an optative and then a bare alternative; the Hebrew keeps both with the jussive יְהִי, so the stanza remains a submission and not a prediction. מָצָב is the glossary's word for a situation or state.
